items.t: How Investors May Respond To NAB Shares After Square Partnership
sum: - National Australia Bank has recently teamed up with Square Australia to link NAB Business Transaction Accounts with Square’s flexible transfer feature, giving eligible business customers more control over when card takings reach their bank accounts.

- The arrangement ties NAB more closely to real time payment flows for small and midsized enterprises and aligns with the bank’s push to deepen business banking relationships and embed its accounts in day to day cash management.
- The focus now shifts to how National Australia Bank's investment narrative fits with this closer Square integration around business cash flow timing.

To own National Australia Bank, you need to be comfortable with a large lender that is leaning into digital payments, business banking and deposit gathering, while still working through cost pressures and a softer recent share price record. The analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St points to earnings growth and technology savings as key supports, and the Square link up broadly fits that direction.

In the short term, the main swing factor remains whether expense growth can be held below revenue growth while asset quality stays contained in business lending. The Square cash flow integration looks helpful but not transformational for these bigger issues, so it probably does not change the near term risk reward balance on its own.

The recent series of wholesale funding deals is the most relevant link here, particularly the £750m floating rate covered bonds due 2030. That transaction, alongside the other sterling and yen issues, feeds into how National Australia Bank funds a balance sheet that is increasingly geared toward digital payments flows and business lending platforms.

For catalysts, investors are watching how efficiently National Australia Bank deploys this funding into its payments and lending projects, including the real time engine that underpins the Square partnership. Execution risk sits in the same place. If technology costs climb faster than planned or business credit losses increase, these new bonds simply increase the importance of getting returns on that spend right.

For investors, the project adds an infrastructure angle to NAB's broader technology spending. National Australia Bank stock: NAB cuts 2027 growth forecast to 1%
sum: National Australia Bank lowered its Australian economic outlook in a report published on November 20, pointing to weaker household spending and business activity. The revised forecast adds a new operating consideration for investors alongside the lender's earnings, funding and credit-quality risks.

The bank now expects Australia's economy to grow by 1% in 2027, compared with its previous forecast of 1.5%. NAB said household consumption growth could slow to 0.7% in 2027, while its latest business survey showed weaker confidence and conditions.

NAB also raised its projected peak-to-trough decline in dwelling values across Australia's combined capital cities to 14%, from 11% previously. The bank expects property prices to stabilise around the middle of 2027, but continued falls would keep household balance sheets and mortgage credit under pressure.

Inflation is forecast to ease, with headline inflation falling from 4.3% in 2026 to 2.8% in 2027 and underlying inflation moderating from 3.6% to 2.9%. NAB expects unemployment to reach 5.4% by the end of 2027 and peak at 5.5% in early 2028.

The bank forecasts the Reserve Bank of Australia will begin gradually reducing its cash rate from August 2027, provided inflation continues to moderate. For NAB, that outlook creates a mixed backdrop: weaker activity may weigh on loan growth and credit quality, while eventual rate cuts could support borrowers and demand.

sum: National Australia Bank reported weaker statutory earnings for the financial year ended September 30, 2026, while maintaining its annual dividend at the previous year's level. In its 5 November results announcement, the bank said cash earnings fell 13.4 percent to 6.141 billion Australian dollars and statutory net profit declined 9.1 percent to 6.143 billion Australian dollars.

The result reflected higher credit impairment charges and large notable items. Credit impairment charges rose to 1.547 billion Australian dollars from 833 million Australian dollars in FY25, while operating expenses increased 18.2 percent after including 1.347 billion Australian dollars of large notable items. Excluding those items, expenses rose 4.5 percent.

NAB said underlying profit excluding large notable items increased 6.9 percent and revenue grew 5.8 percent. Net interest margin improved by six basis points to 1.80 percent, while gross loans and deposits each increased 5.2 percent. The bank said lending competition partly offset the benefit from higher earnings on deposits and capital-related portfolios.

The quality of the result varied across divisions. Cash earnings excluding large notable items rose 10.7 percent in Business and Private Banking to 3.685 billion Australian dollars and increased 8.7 percent in Personal Banking to 1.362 billion Australian dollars. ASX bank shares such as NAB need deposits and good profit margins to make their business profitable. Meaning, a bank gets money from term deposit holders and wholesale debt investors and lends that money to homeowners, businesses and investors. The difference between what a bank pays to savers and what it makes from mortgage holders (for example) is the net interest margin or NIM. Remember: when it comes to NIMs, the wider the margin the better.

If you are planning to estimate the profits of a bank like NAB or ANZ Banking Group (ASX: ANZ), knowing how much money the bank lends and what it makes per dollar lent to borrowers is crucial. Some experts will try to tell you that ‘the lower PE ratio is better’ because it means the share price is ‘low’ relative to the profits produced by the company. However, sometimes shares are cheap for a reason!
Secondly, some extremely successful companies have gone for many years (a decade or more) and never reported an accounting profit — so the PE ratio can’t be used to value them.
Therefore, we think it’s crucial to dig deeper than just looking at the PE ratio and thinking to yourself ‘if it’s below 10x, I’ll buy it.’

One of the easy ratio models analysts use to value a bank share is to compare the PE ratio of the bank/share you’re looking at with its peer group or competitors and try to determine if the share is too much or cheap relative to the average. From there, and using the principle of mean reversion, we can multiply the profits/earnings per share by the sector average (E x sector PE) to reflect what an average company would be worth. It’s like saying, ‘if all of the other stocks are priced at ‘X’, this one should be too’.

items.t: Who will get left holding the banks?
sum: The major banks have been the mainstay of the domestic investment landscape in Australia for over 100 years. While credit cycles have come and gone, as the country has prospered and the population has grown, the banks have been a major beneficiary. Currently Australia’s top five companies by market capitalisation are the four major retail banks and BHP. The prominence of the banks is a phenomenon that has long been the case. In fact, looking at the largest 10 companies by market capitalisation every five years since 1990 demonstrates the longevity of this dominance. As a result, the banks make up a very large proportion of the exposure most Australians have to domestic equities. ANZ, Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and Westpac constitute 22.6% of the ASX200.

The question is, should investors be this invested in the sector? Or, for the first time in a very long time, is there a competitive threat for the banks’ profits and business model emerging that the market might be underestimating?

For most of the last 50 years the fundamentals of banking have not changed a great deal. A bank is a relatively simple proposition. You need funding, which is typically in the form of a combination of bank capital, wholesale funding and deposits from clients with savings. The funding mix is influenced by regulatory capital requirements and the cost of the relative sources of funding. And then you lend this capital to borrowers. You charge borrowers more than you pay those providing the funding, with the bank earning the spread between these two rates, which is called the net interest margin. You then have expenses, such as employee, property, technology, marketing, commission, utilities and regulatory costs. There are also expected credit losses and realised losses on loans that have gone into default and are unable to be repaid in full. Deducting these expenses from the net interest margin earned and any revenue earned from trading and fees charged to clients gives you profit before tax.

The largest four domestic banks have a combined market share of over 70% of gross assets held by financial institutions in the domestic market. As a result, these banks have had significant scale advantages that increase profitability.
